title: The cell nucleus – chromosomes, chromosome structure, DNA, RNA
blurb: Introduces the course and its exam (24-question test, lectures only, 3 terms).
h1: The cell nucleus – chromosomes, chromosome structure, DNA, RNA
lede: Introduces the course and its exam (24-question test, lectures only, 3 terms). Then covers karyology: what a karyotype is, how chromosome number, size and shape vary, and chromosome mutations. Next come genome size (C-value, the C-value paradox), polyploidy (auto- vs allo-) and aneuploidy (mono-, nulli-, tri-, tetrasomy), and how plants and animals tolerate them. The second half covers nucleic acids: the history of the DNA structure, nucleotide composition, phosphodiester bonds, complementary base pairing, DNA vs RNA, the three types of RNA, and the central dogma.
six: Definitions: karyotype, C-value, euchromatin vs heterochromatin, polyploidy vs aneuploidy
Auto- vs allopolyploidy, with an example each
A–T 2 H-bonds, C–G 3 H-bonds; purines vs pyrimidines

questions.q: How many questions does the Fundamentals of Biology exam test have?
questions.e: Slide 3: the exam is a test of 24 questions based only on the lectures. (Slides: p. 3)

questions.q: Which type of chromatin is transcriptionally active?
questions.e: Euchromatin is active; heterochromatin is very dense and inactive. (Slides: p. 7)

questions.q: A diploid organism that has lost a whole homologous pair of chromosomes is:
questions.e: Nullisomy = 2n − 2, loss of a homologous pair. (Slides: p. 19)

questions.q: Galeopsis tetrahit (2n = 4x = 32) arose from G. pubescens × G. speciosa. This is an example of:
questions.e: Hybridisation of two species followed by genome doubling = allopolyploidy. (Slides: p. 26)

questions.answer: the amount of DNA in a haploid nucleus
wrong: the number of chromosomes in a somatic cell
the number of genes in a genome
the ratio of coding to non-coding DNA
questions.e: C-value = DNA amount in a haploid nucleus (gamete). (Slides: p. 14)

questions.q: The C-value paradox refers to the fact that:
questions.answer: genome size does not correlate with organismal complexity
wrong: all eukaryotes have the same genome size
prokaryotes have larger genomes than eukaryotes
questions.e: Some protists have much larger genomes than humans. (Slides: p. 16)

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds form between cytosine and guanine?
questions.e: C–G has 3 H-bonds, A–T has 2. (Slides: p. 37)

questions.q: Which of the following is a purine?
questions.e: Purines are A and G; pyrimidines are C, T and U. (Slides: p. 32)

questions.q: Which RNA transfers a specific amino acid to the growing polypeptide chain?
questions.e: tRNA (transfer RNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome. (Slides: p. 40)

questions.q: Who received the 1962 Nobel Prize for the structure of nucleic acids?
questions.e: The prize went to Crick, Watson and Maurice Wilkins. (Slides: p. 29)

questions.q: In animals, which change in genome size is always lethal?
questions.answer: loss of more than 5 % or excess of more than 10 %
questions.e: Loss > 5 % or excess > 10 % of the genome is always lethal. (Slides: p. 20)

questions.q: The phosphodiester bond in the DNA backbone links:
questions.answer: the 3′-OH of one sugar and the 5′-phosphate of the next
wrong: the 5′-OH of one sugar and the 3′-phosphate of the next base
questions.e: The 3′ hydroxyl and 5′ phosphate of adjacent sugars. (Slides: p. 35)

cards.lede: Read the question, answer it out loud, then flip the card.

items.a: The number and appearance of chromosomes in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell.
The branch of cytology dealing with the structure of cell nuclei, especially chromosomes.
Euchromatin is transcriptionally active DNA; heterochromatin is very dense and transcriptionally inactive.

items.n: With which proteins is DNA packed into chromatin?
items.a: Histones.

items.n: Who first observed chromosomes, and when?
items.a: Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli, in plant cells, 1842.
Walther Flemming (1882, salamander cells).

items.n: What does 2n mean, and what does n mean?
items.a: 2n = chromosome number in somatic cells; n = number in gametes.
The number of chromosomes in the ancestral (non-homologous) basic set; may differ from n.

items.n: Which plant has the lowest chromosome number?
items.a: Haplopappus gracilis, 2n = 4.

items.n: Which organism has more than 1200 chromosomes?
items.a: The fern Ophioglossum reticulatum.

items.n: Name the 4 chromosome shapes by centromere position.
items.a: Telocentric, acrocentric, submetacentric, metacentric.
Single: deletion, duplication, inversion. Two-chromosome: insertion, translocation.
The amount of DNA in a haploid nucleus (gamete), i.e. half the diploid somatic amount.

items.n: 1 pg of DNA equals how many base pairs?
items.a: 978 Mbp.
Genlisea aurea 0.065 pg/1C; Paris japonica 152.23 pg/1C.
Genome size does not correlate with organismal complexity (e.g. some protists have larger genomes than humans).
No.
A nucleotide sequence within a gene removed by RNA splicing during RNA maturation.
Having more than two paired (homologous) sets of chromosomes.
Presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell.

items.n: What genome change is always lethal in animals?
items.a: Loss of more than 5 % or excess of more than 10 % of the genome.
No significant consequences; mono-/nullisomics have lower vitality and fertility.
Dactylis polygama 2n=2x=14 → D. glomerata 2n=4x=28 (also Alnus glutinosa → A. rohlenae).
Galeopsis pubescens × G. speciosa (2n=16 each) → G. tetrahit 2n=4x=32.

items.n: What share of major crop production comes from polyploids?
Where is DNA located in the cell?
items.a: Nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts.

items.n: Who published the DNA double helix, where and when?
items.a: Watson and Crick, Nature, 25 April 1953 (Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge).

items.n: Who received the 1962 Nobel Prize for DNA structure?
items.a: Francis Crick, James Watson and Maurice Wilkins.

items.n: Whose X-ray data guided Watson and Crick?
items.a: Rosalind Franklin's (images taken by her student Raymond Gosling).
Nitrogenous base, sugar (deoxyribose/ribose), phosphate group.

items.n: Which bases are purines and which pyrimidines?
items.a: Purines: A, G. Pyrimidines: C, T, U.

items.n: Between which atoms is the phosphodiester bond?
items.a: The 3′-OH of one sugar and the 5′-phosphate of the next.

items.n: How many hydrogen bonds in A–T and in C–G?
items.a: A–T 2; C–G 3.

items.n: Which two forces stabilise the double helix?
items.a: Hydrogen bonds between bases and base-stacking interactions.

items.n: Three differences between RNA and DNA?
items.a: RNA is mostly single-stranded and shorter, has ribose, and has uracil instead of thymine.
mRNA carries protein sequence info to ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids; rRNA + protein form the ribosome.
Synthesis of DNA from an RNA template (RNA → DNA).
